title: USB phone charger: safe teardown
summary: A working USB wall charger is worth more whole than in pieces. A dead one gives a 400 V capacitor, a fuse, a small transformer, an optocoupler and a USB socket. Its mains-side capacitor can hold up to about 340 V after unplugging: discharge it and prove it dead before you touch the board, and never plug an opened charger back into the mains.

steps.text: Test it first. Plug it into a working socket and charge a phone with it, or measure DC volts between the two outer pins of its USB-A socket: you want about 5 V. Read the input range on the label too. A working charger is worth keeping whole: if it works, stop here and don't open it. Unplug it.
steps.warn: Only plug in a charger whose case is whole and uncracked. Hold the meter probes by their guards.

steps.text: Unplug it and leave it for at least 5 minutes. From here on it never goes back into a socket.
Look for screws under labels or rubber feet. Many small chargers have none: the two halves of the shell are glued or welded together (the Anker and Samsung chargers here are ultrasonically welded).

Crack the seam. No cited source shows a way into a welded shell (Shirriff used a rotary tool), so go slowly. Hold the charger in a vice or clamp with cloth over the jaws, pressing across the seam, and tighten a little at a time, turning it, until the seam splits. Or cut round the seam with a fine saw, only as deep as the shell wall. Then work a flat screwdriver into the seam to part the halves, with the charger held fast in the clamp, never in your free hand. Keep both hands behind the tip and push away from your body.
steps.warn: Wear glasses and gloves: the shell can split with a crack and throw pieces, and a slipped screwdriver or saw goes into your hand. Saw away from you, and keep the blade out of the board and the capacitors.

steps.text: Ease the board out with one hand, holding it by its edges and keeping your fingers off the solder side and the capacitor leads, and set it down solder side up on dry wood or card. If wires to the mains pins hold it, cut them. Leave any glue or white compound on the parts.
steps.warn: Don't touch the solder side, the capacitor leads or the pin contacts until the capacitor has been discharged and measured.

steps.text: Find the mains side: the end wired to the pins, with a fuse or striped fusible resistor, the rectifier, and one or two electrolytic capacitors marked 400 V. Then find the isolation gap: a slot or bare strip across the board that only the transformer, a small optocoupler chip and a blue disc capacitor (the Y capacitor) cross.

First check your meter works: set it to DC volts and read a battery. Then discharge each 400 V capacitor with the resistor tool from safety_discharge_capacitor (2–5 kΩ, 10 W or more): clip one lead on, touch the probe to the other lead and hold it there for 10 seconds, holding only the insulated parts. Now measure DC volts across each capacitor. Under 1 V is safe to touch; if it reads more, discharge again. Twist a bare wire across its leads and leave it there until you unsolder it.
steps.warn: These capacitors charge to about 1.4 times the mains voltage, up to about 340 V DC, and a broken charger may not drain them. Measure every time. Never short them with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Unsolder the parts you want: the 400 V capacitors, the fuse or fusible resistor, the optocoupler, the USB socket and the transformer. Free all the transformer's pins with solder wick or by heating them in turn, then lift it gently.
steps.warn: The transformer's ferrite core is brittle and cracks if you lever it.

steps.text: Twist a bare wire across the leads of each 400 V capacitor, then bag the parts from each charger together with a note of its label rating. Keep the Y capacitor only as a like-for-like replacement Y capacitor.
steps.warn: Only a Y-rated capacitor may cross an isolation gap. An ordinary capacitor there can put mains voltage on the USB lead.

steps.text: Throw away the shell and anything that cracked. Never rebuild an opened charger and plug it into the mains.
steps.warn: Opening it can tear insulation or bend parts across the isolation gap without you seeing. A charger that fails that way can put mains voltage on the USB lead.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **A working charger, whole.** A 5 V USB supply wherever there is mains from a generator or inverter, for phones, radios, lights and LoRa nodes. USB-C fast chargers also give higher voltages to devices that ask for them: the Anker A2633 is labelled 5 V 3 A and 9 V 2.22 A (iFixit Anker A2633), the Samsung EP-TA800 5 V 3 A and 9 V 2.77 A (Chongdiantou Samsung EP-TA800). For 12 V systems, car USB chargers are the better fit (build_usb_charging_station).
- **400 V capacitors.** Two 10 µF 400 V in the A2633 (iFixit Anker A2633); 22 µF and 15 µF, both 400 V, in the EP-TA800 (Chongdiantou Samsung EP-TA800). Spares for repairing other chargers and LED drivers: replace like with like, same value and at least the same voltage.
- **Fuse or fusible resistor.** A 2 A 250 V time-delay fuse in the A2633 (iFixit Anker A2633), a 10 Ω fusible resistor in the Apple A1265 (Shirriff Apple A1265), and a 1.1 Ω 2 W fusible resistor in the EP-TA800 (Chongdiantou Samsung EP-TA800). Spares for the same kind of supply.
- **Optocoupler.** An LED and a light sensor sealed in one small chip, so a signal crosses a gap with no wire. It can let a small controller switch or sense another circuit safely apart from it.
- **Transformer.** A small ferrite transformer. Apple's has a high-voltage primary, a small auxiliary winding and an output winding of triple-insulated wire (Shirriff Apple A1265). Only useful for rebuilding the same kind of supply.
- **USB socket.** For a home-made USB outlet on a 5 V supply.

## Isolation: why an opened charger stays off the mains

- A charger's main safety job is keeping mains away from the USB plug. Ken Shirriff gives about 4 mm as the separation standards call for. Apple's A1265 had about 6 mm, crossed only by the transformer, the optocouplers and the Y capacitor, which is marked X1 400 V and Y1 250 V and which Shirriff tentatively reads as 220 pF (Shirriff Apple A1265).
- The Samsung EP-TA800 has a slot cut in the board under its optocoupler to keep a 6 mm gap (Chongdiantou Samsung EP-TA800).
- A fake iPhone charger had an average gap of only about 1 mm and single layers of tape in its transformer where two were required. Shirriff says it has 340 V DC inside, enough to kill, and that a short could send lethal voltage through the USB cable (Shirriff fake charger).
- Cracking a welded shell and flexing the board can break these barriers in ways you can't see. That is why an opened charger is parts only.

## Variations

- **Apple A1265 (5 V 1 A, about 2012):** two boards, with two large electrolytic capacitors smoothing the rectified mains (Shirriff Apple A1265). Its mains-side voltage reaches about 340 V DC.
- **Anker A2633 (20 W USB-C):** shell sealed by ultrasonic welding, three small boards, parts held with glue, and one controller chip working both sides of the gap (iFixit Anker A2633). The unit iFixit opened was labelled for 200–240 V input only, so check the input range before using a charger from another country.
- **Samsung EP-TA800 (25 W USB-C):** welded shell, parts potted in compound, and a flat (planar) transformer glued to the board (Chongdiantou Samsung EP-TA800).

## What to leave

- **The shell.** Cracked plastic, no use.
- **Tiny surface-mount chips and potted parts.** Too small or too stuck to reuse by hand.
- **A transformer whose core cracked.** Shirriff's broke during disassembly (Shirriff Apple A1265).
- **The Y capacitor,** except as a like-for-like replacement.

## Testing what you got out

- **Capacitors:** see test_capacitor.
- **Fuse or fusible resistor:** a continuity or low ohms reading means it is whole (test_continuity).
- **Optocoupler:** on diode test, its LED pins read like a diode one way and open the other way.
